To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

all motion‐ sensitive neurons in the pigeon pretectum respond to illusory motion, and some of them produce after‐responses to the cessation of prolonged motion, which is similar to the motion after‐ effect reported in humans.

the pretectal neurons of pigeons respond to illusory and real contours in the same way, that they show motion after‐responses to the cessation of prolonged motion, and that the time course of the after‐responses resembles the motion after‐effects reported by humans.

the motion‐sensitive pretectal neurons respond similarly to real versus illusORY contours, and some of them produce inhibitory after‐responses to the cessation of prolonged motion, which may underlie the motion after‐eFECT.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neuronal mechanisms underlying visual illusions in the pigeon's brain.
the neuronal basis of visual illusions, which may be a useful model to understand the neural mechanism of visual perception.
the neuronal mechanisms of visual illusions and the motion after‐effects in lower brain centers.

illusory contour and motion are processed at the earliest stage, and the motion after‐response results from functional interaction of excitatory and inhibititory receptive fields with the opposite directionalities.
visual illusions can be processed at the earliest stages of visual processing and in the lower parts of the visual system.
the motion after-effect is not a perceptual illusion, but a real physiological phenomenon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
illusory visual information is detected at an early stage of information processing in the central nervous system and is processed in the same way as real visual information.

The main takeaway from our work is that
visual illusions can be processed in early brain areas, and that the neuronal mechanisms underlying illusory contours may be similar in lower and higher brain areas.
illusory motion is detected by the brain in the pretectum, and that the mechanisms for illusory motion are similar to the mechanisms for motion in the real world.
the motion after-effect is not an illusion, and that illusory motion is a real motion.
